newsitem.title: TURKEY: Bankers confident about new Turkish cash pool.
newsitem.headline: Bankers confident about new Turkish cash pool.

text.p: Turkey's recent step to pool all public revenues under a central cash management would help the government to increase its control on state funds but not affect the financial system, bankers said on Tuesday.
Officials from state-owned banks said there were uncertainities over the use of the pool account because they have not signed any protocol with the treasury to clarify technical details.
A senior economy bureacurat said the new system was an intervention in the free-market economy.

"The government's new regulations to pool the public revenues is an intervention to the system. The state enterprises should increase their revenues according to free market system. But they are forced to hold their cash at state banks," the official who asked not to be named told Reuters.

Under the new regulation which took effect from November 1, all state economic enterprises would close their own time deposit acconts at maturity and transfer their cash to two separate pools of foreign currency and Turkish lira.
Four state banks -- Ziraat Bankas, Halkbank, Emlakbank and Vakfbank -- have opened a pool account for the Turkish lira and foreign currency and started to collect cash from state institutions.

The public enterprises will not be allowed to draw cash from the pool accounts, open new savings accounts of their own and make repurchase agreements on the bond market without the permission of the treasury.
Shortly after a financial crisis in early 1994, Turkey had put a regulation into effect, asking state enterprises to hold their accounts at public banks.
But there was no restriction on repurchase agreements and some public institutions held their cash at private banks despite the regulation.
"Most of about 400 trillion lira public cash is held at state banks. So this new regulation will not result in a cash withdrawal from private banks in the short-run," a state-banker said.

"If the treasury uses this pool to meet its domestic debt servicing or the politicians try to use that account for political goals that will cause some problems and raise interest rates in the system," he added.

"The government has now the opportunity to see and control all the public revenue at one account. This is good and will not affect markets," said a securities manager at a leading private bank. --Istanbul newsroom +90-212-275 08 75 ATA
